Mr. President, Colombia is now facing, as many other countries as we have here today, a different form of terrorism. It evolves. Therefore, and that explains in a great, great way why it's so difficult to find a common definition. But we should not be in the wrong side of history, given the difficulties, the particularities that each of one of us face. It is not impossible to get there. What happened is that terrorism works differently and actually uses the failures of the systems to evolve. It's combined and of course, is as well international. In the case of Colombia, the most recent phenomenon is the illegal mining. an activity that appears in other countries legal, in our country is used to foster the financial resources for terrorist groups in our country. It's also an activity that is combined now with drug trafficking. The combination of the two is lethal. Colombia is facing a great challenge and our government is fighting with all that we have and must within the law, within our constitution, and within the international law to defeat a problem that uses terrorism to destroy generations and the future of our country and many others. There are also human rights consequences of terrorism. After 9/11, 141 countries changed all their national security laws. It was a trend, and of course, it followed by the terrorist attacks across the planet. Yet, we don't have a singular, definition of what terrorism is about, and we think that this is truly the issue at stake, when actually it's not. Colombia presents to you a basic proposal, otherwise we will not reach that consensus. It seems that we have different scopes to define terrorism. We should select those that are common to all of us, to our history, to our cultures, to our reality, to our geopolitics. And what appears common was given here to us in 9/11. We have always learned about the stories of those that did the unimaginable, but also must remember the force of the victims that exhibited the greatest bravery that we have remembered. It was an equation of those that were brave against those that are cowards. Cowardice is a characteristic that is common. Terrorism is a vehicle in and of itself and can be and must be stopped. The only way to get to this common definition is to recognize the core elements of terrorism as the central legal equation to define what is simply clear to all of us unacceptable. We can define by degrees and assign accountability, but the relationships that go to the core of terrorism, the financing, of course, the technology. Colombia, press on you the urgency to pay close attention to one of the greatest challenge, which is not AI, but is what is known as the final core. We are arriving in a time that quantum technology and AI meet. Ineluctably, the design of the algorithm will define nothing else than humanity. And terrorism uses not the capabilities but the failures and the weaknesses of the system. And when it comes to technology, the world is about to know other type of terrorism. And this time, we cannot be in the wrong side of history. We call upon the United Nations Security Council to advance further with the resolutions 2462, 1568, and build at least an approach by scopes of terrorism that integrates different realities and allow us to strike directly where the world needs. Mr. President.

For my country, for Latin America as a region, what occurred on the 11th of September in the USA has a clear ideological structure underpinning it, but it also had undeniable consequences. the United States of America and the peoples of Latin America have historic ties and many Latin American people lived or continue to live and they are still here indeed in the United States of America. We lost many of them, however. For our region, for Colombia, It is crucial for us to act, for us to use, leverage the sanctions regime. We can show the world that this is a problem where there is common ground. The scope of the phenomenon can vary, as can our approaches. However, we can return to crucial common ground. What we cannot do is hesitate. We cannot balk. We must act with resolve.

Technology goes really fast, and we must act as well in the same direction with the same pace.

It is vital for the future of humankind that we act that we reach consensus at least, and this is the key appeal of the Republic of Colombia to you. Colombia as a country that has lost thousands and thousands of people over the last 40, 50 years in which it has fought against terrorism. We fought against guerrillas, paramilitaries, drug dealers. We are doing our part. and we will do everything we can, everything in our power, but we need the assistance of the United Nations and of the Security Council, just as many other countries do, just as many other people do. We must do everything we can. We owe that to future generations, but also to victims. We appeal to you all for us to continue these efforts in spite of our differences. We must understand that together we can garner consensus. Mr. President, with a thank you briefest today. It's been 25 years today since the monstrous terrorist attacks in the United States that claimed the lives of nearly 3,000 innocent people. We would like to once again, would like to express our sincere condolences to the people of the United States of America, as well as to the relatives and loved ones of those who perished. Among them were citizens of dozens of states, including Russians. The tragedy of the September 11th showed very clearly that terrorism knows no borders, does not distinguish its victims by nationality, religion, or citizenship. And our country has more than once become a target of terrorists in Beslan, in Nordost, the bombings in the Moscow Metro, and the attack on Crocus City Hall. have left deep wounds in the memory of the Russian people. And behind each of these crimes are those who were killed and injured, shattered lives, and families for whom lives changed forever. We understand well what terrorists are seeking to achieve. Their goal is not only to take human lives, but also to sow fear, to divide societies, and to drive states apart. In September 2001, this calculation failed. The international community was able to unite in the face of a common tragedy. The Security Council responded swiftly and decisively. On the 20th of September 2001, already, the landmark resolution 1373 was adopted unanimously, which established the Security Council Counter-Terrorism Committee. This document became one of the cornerstones of the modern international counter-terrorism architecture. Russia supported this and other key Security Council decisions in response to the terrorist attacks and joined the practical cooperation in the field of counterterrorism. Over the following quarter century, the international architecture created at that time underwent significant developments. The Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate was established. Mechanisms were formed for assessing States' implementation of their obligations and identifying their needs for technical assistance. Mechanisms were created for countering the financing of terrorism and the cross-border movement of foreign terrorist fighters. Efforts against extremist ideology were strengthened. The sanctions regime against ISIL and al-Qaeda continue to be improved. In 2006, the United Nations Global Counterterrorism Strategy was adopted by consensus, and in 2017, the United Nations Office of Counterterrorism was established, and it was assigned the leading role in coordinating the counterterrorism efforts of the UN system and providing relevant technical assistance to states. These instruments remain in demand today because the terrorist threat has not disappeared. Quite to the contrary, it is becoming increasingly complex and adaptive. ISIL and affiliated structures remain active in the Middle East and are expanding their presence in some areas of Africa. ISIL-Khorasan in Afghanistan continues to pose a serious danger. And the problem of foreign terrorist fighters, capable of transferring the combat experience they have acquired from one region to another, has not lost its relevance. At the same time, the terrorist toolkit is changing. Modern technologies enable them to recruit supporters, to disseminate propaganda, raise funds, coordinate their actions, and prepare attacks while being thousands of kilometers apart. Terrorist groups are making ever greater use of digital financial instruments, drones, AI, and new means of communication. All of these threats are transboundary in nature and require a coordinated international response. No state, regardless of the capabilities at its disposal, is able effectively to counter terrorism on its own. Mr. President, Against this background, particular concern is caused by the continuing obstacles to full-fledged international counterterrorism cooperation. In a number of key areas, cooperation today is not being strengthened, but, to the contrary, is encountering additional difficulties. And we see this especially clearly in the sphere of information sharing, coordination amongst competent authorities, and the practical application of mutual legal assistance mechanisms. This is not an abstract problem. Any delay in transmitting information, disruption of work contacts, or inability to obtain necessary data in a timely manner creates vulnerabilities that terrorist structures can exploit. Terrorists long ago learned to operate at the intersection of jurisdictions and to exploit differences in national legislation, financial systems, and approaches to law enforcement cooperation. the weaker the interaction among states, the broader the opportunities for militants. Today, international relations are going through a difficult period. On many issues, states' positions differ significantly. However, the fight against terrorism must not become a hostage to geopolitical confrontation. The price of weakened cooperation in this sphere is measured not in political costs, but in human lives. Mr. President, September 11, is not only a day of remembrance of those who perished. It's also a reminder of how important unity and coordinated action by states are in the face of a common threat. Since 2001, we have succeeded in building an effective system of counterterrorism cooperation. Today, it is important not only to preserve the effectiveness of this system, but also to increase its resilience to political turbulence. and its ability to respond in a timely manner to new forms and manifestations of the terrorist threat. Russia consistently advocates professional and depoliticized counterterrorism cooperation on the basis of the norms and principles of international law. Priorities. must remain the timely and uninterrupted exchange of information, mutual legal assistance, working contacts among competent authorities, and the joint development of responses to evolving methods of terrorist activity. Terrorists always seek to exploit division, mistrust, and lack of coordination among states. Our response must be exactly the opposite: unity of approaches, mutual trust, and readiness to act together where the protection of human lives and common security is concerned. And this is one of the principal lessons of September 11th and our duty to those whom we remember today. I thank you.
I thank the representative of the Russian Federation and I give the floor to the representative of the Russian Federation.

Thank you, President. At the outset, I would like to thank Ms. Gurman, Executive Director of the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate. and to Mr. Ihab Ameish, Director for Policy and Coordination at the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism, and to Ms. Noreen Fink, the Executive Director of GIFCT. I thank them for their valuable briefings. Mr. President, we meet today on a solemn occasion. As we mark the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks that took place in the United States on September 11, we remember their innocent victims, as well as all victims of terrorism around the world. In the aftermath of the terrorist attacks of September 11, the Security Council adopted a number of resolutions, including Resolution 1373, which laid the foundation for the international counter-terrorism architecture and established obligations for all Member States alike to combat and suppress terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. We have recently reached an important milestone. as this year marks the 20th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Global Counter-Strategy Terrorism. This strategy sent a clear message against terrorism and serves as a global reference and a comprehensive framework for preventing and combating terrorism in all its forms. Mr. President, the Kingdom of Bahrain and the countries of the region have recently been subjected to terrorist attacks targeting their territories and civilian and vital facilities, within the context of Iran's practices that threaten Bahrain's security and the stability of the region. These acts constitute a serious escalation that requires a collective response, reflecting the priority the Council places on the maintenance of international peace and security. Accordingly, the Kingdom of Bahrain reiterates the need for Iran to fully comply with the relevant Security Council resolutions, particularly resolution 2817, and to cease all attacks hostile acts and threats affecting the security of the countries of the region and undermining de-escalation efforts. Iran should also respect the sovereignty of states and adhere to the principles of good neighborliness and to refrain from any practices that could undermine regional security and stability. Mr. President, terrorism remains one of the most significant threats to international peace and security. Despite ongoing efforts to combat terrorism, the terrorist threat persists, and it continues to evolve, taking new forms and methods, while exploiting technological advances and emerging environments. In this regard, I would like to focus on the following points. First, The security environment is undergoing rapid changes driven by new and emerging technologies, particularly in the fields of artificial intelligence, drones, cryptocurrencies, and virtual assets. The Kingdom of Bahrain expresses its concern over the use of digital platforms for the dissemination of extremist propaganda, recruitment, incitement, fundraising, and the planning of terrorist operations. We therefore call for a continued examination of these challenges, while at the same time harnessing modern technologies to strengthen efforts to prevent and combat terrorism. We emphasize the importance of a greater engagement by the Council on these issues. Second, the Kingdom of Bahrain stresses the need to work seriously to deny terrorists access to sources of financing and to strengthen efforts aimed at combating terrorist financing, including the misuse of digital wallets, virtual assets and cryptocurrencies to conceal the identities of beneficial owners. The Kingdom also emphasizes the importance of the effective implementation of the recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force, FATF, as well as strengthening financial intelligence capabilities, cooperation and information sharing among states. Third, the Kingdom of Bahrain emphasizes the need to take practical and concrete steps to enhance international cooperation, information sharing and capacity building. while ensuring the full and effective implementation of the Council's sanctions regimes and the regular updating of sanctions lists in order to keep pace with the evolving terrorist threats. In conclusion, the Kingdom of Bahrain reaffirms its steadfast commitment to preventing and combating terrorism, implementing relevant Security Council resolutions, and continuing to work with all partners to combat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, to dry up its sources of financing, and to address the threat it poses to international peace and security. Thank you, President.
I thank the representative of Bahrain for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Latvia.

Thank you, Mr. President. First, I would like to commend France for convening the Council today, just like the French Presidency did it 25 years ago in September. And I also wish to thank our briefers for their contributions. 25 years have passed since the tragic morning of September 11, 2001. And yet, for so many, September 11 does not feel like history. It remains a date marked by absence, by families who still carry an empty place at the table, by the first responders who never came home, and by a world that on that day came to realize with painful clarity how terrorism can profoundly threaten human life, trust, international peace and security. Today, we stand with the people of the United States. We remember nearly 3,000 people who lost their lives in New York, Washington, DC, Arlington, Virginia, and Pennsylvania. Not as statistics, but as mothers and fathers, sons and daughters, colleagues, friends, and citizens of a world that believed it was safe. We also remember all those affected by terrorism in the years since, in cities and communities across the world. Their suffering reminds that terrorism knows no borders and respects no nationality. For Latvia, like many other nations, 9/11 became a moment of assuming collective responsibility for terrorism's threat to international peace and security. In the aftermath of the attacks, we joined the International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan as part of this Council's mandated effort. And also, our contribution came at a cost. Latvian soldiers served far from home, alongside our allies, and some of them never returned. Today, Latvia also remembers them. Today, we remember that behind every international commitment are human beings who are willing to stand in harm's way in the hope that others may live in greater security. The United Nations, too, was changed by September 11. Within weeks, Also under the French presidency, this Council unanimously adopted resolution 1373, establishing a comprehensive international framework for combating terrorism, creating the Counter-Terrorism Committee and 1267 sanctions regime. Since then, the United Nations counter-terrorism mechanisms have continued to strengthen international cooperation and support national capacity building to prevent terrorism financing, curb movement of foreign terrorist fighters, improve border security, and counter radicalization. 25 years on, the fight against terrorism is far from over. The threat landscape has changed and evolved. A wealth of new technology, accessible and affordable worldwide, has changed and in many ways eased the way terrorists operate. Terrorist groups in remote areas of the world can use commercial satellites, digital financial tools, use encrypted messages to coordinate attacks, order parts of UAVs online, or use AI to reach communities in any language to spread propaganda and recruit new members. And while we are discussing emerging use of new technologies, in fact, artificial intelligence, commercial satellites, virtual currencies, crypto assets, UAVs are enthusiastically and widely embraced by individual terrorists and terrorist groups. So we call for a clear, direct approach that recognizes these challenges while exploring ways to harness technology in compliance with international law to counter terrorism. 25 years after 9/11, the greatest tribute we can offer to victims and survivors of terrorist attacks worldwide are to remember the unity in which we came together after the Twin Towers came down. In our conviction to never let this happen again, we came together to design a robust international normative framework and tools required to take on new challenges as they emerge on the counterterrorism landscape. So this Council needs to recognize that the new age of technology is already upon us. and that we need to take action to strengthen the collective response to terrorism. So we commend France for focusing this meeting not only on commemoration, but looking ahead to the future and setting the pace for resolute Council action against the fast-evolving threat of terrorism worldwide.

I thank you. I thank the representative of Latvia for the statement. I shall now make a statement in my capacity as a representative for France.

I first of all wish to thank the Executive Director of the Counter-Terrorism Committee, Ms. Natalia German, as well as the Director for Policy and Coordination at the UN OCT, Mr. Ayoub Maish, and the Executive Director of the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism, Ms. Chowdhury Fink. I thank them all for briefings which illustrate both the persistent nature and evolution of the threat. They also pave the way towards an effective response. Everyone remembers where he was on the 11th of September 2001, when the Twin Towers were struck by an unprecedented terrorist attack. More than 3,000 people lost their lives that day. Today, we pay tribute to the victims, to their families, to the city of New York, and to the United States and the American people, indeed, 25 years after this deadly attack. France has not been spared by terrorism. We do not forget the victims of the Bataclan, Saint-Denis, Charlie Hebdo, Nice and so many other attacks elsewhere. Very few countries have not fallen victim to terrorism. The memory of 11 September, as well as that of all terrorist attacks throughout the world, must remind us of our responsibility and that of this Council to fight collectively against the terrorist threat. Yes, the fight against terrorism is at the heart of the Security Council's mission. In 2001, the Council proved able to act quickly and with resolve. Indeed, the day after the attacks, the Security Council adopted resolution 1368, condemning the attack and committing to take necessary measures against this scourge. This commitment was upheld by resolution 1373, which was also adopted unanimously on the 28th of September 2001. It enshrines all states' obligation to suppress terrorism and creates dedicated mechanism for international cooperation in this regard, the CTC. In 25 years, the Security Council has established a robust normative framework to dry up terrorist financing, to restrict terrorist movements, to thwart their recruitment strategies. These norms scrupulously respect human rights and the rule of law. and go hand in hand with actions on the root causes of terrorism, actions to prevent violent extremism and actions to counter radicalization. France is fully committed to the fight against terrorism. We participated in the coalition in Afghanistan from 2001 onwards. We've fought subsidiaries of al-Qaeda in the Sahel and we remain mobilised within the international coalition against Daesh in the Middle East. I wish to pay tribute to soldiers who have perished in all operations against terrorism. Our fight is far from over. Terrorism goes hand in hand with our society's progress because it weaponises our own innovations against us. Daesh, al-Qaeda and their affiliates continue to expand their presence and conduct cross-border attacks far from their bases. Daesh is strengthening its foothold in the African continent, the Sahel, in the DRC and in East Africa. In the Middle East, terrorist groups seize the slightest opportunity to carve out a safe haven. In Afghanistan, Daesh-Khorasan is one of the most active branches of the organization. Terrorists have changed their modus operandi. They instrumentalize and divert new technologies, drones, commercial satellites, artificial intelligence, to conduct more targeted and more deadly attacks. They hone professional propaganda methods. They attract ever younger recruits. And they fully harness new finance technologies. The Council's action over the last 25 years has served to unite the international community against terrorism. we must once again play this role as a driver. This involves putting in place an effective system to fight against the use of new technologies by terrorism. The presidential statement that we will adopt today is an expression of the Council in this regard. It is incumbent upon all of us collectively to ensure that a tragedy such as that of September the 11th never again occurs. I thank you. I now resume my function as President of the Council. The Council has the text before it of a presidential statement. It was the text of a statement by the President on behalf of the Council on the subject of today's meeting. I thank Council members for their valuable contributions to this statement. In accordance with the understanding reached among members of the Council, shall I take it that members of the Security Council agree to the statement, which will be issued as a document of the Security Council under the symbol S/PRST/1200. There are no more speakers on my list. I wish to thank our briefers, and the meeting is adjourned.
